UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
) 
Docket No. EL25-49-000 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating 
Facilities 
) 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
v. 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
 
) 
 
) 
Docket No. EL25-20-000 
(consolidated) 
 
ANSWER OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS  
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 2131 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) and the Commission’s Show Cause 
Order,2 the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (hereinafter, “Indicated TOs”)3 submit this 
 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2024). 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at Ordering Paragraph (D) (2025) (“Show Cause Order”). 
3 The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners include: American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf of 
Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power 
Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP Appalachian Transmission Company, Inc., AEP 
Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Kentucky Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission 
Company, Inc., and AEP West Virginia Transmission Company, Inc.; AMP Transmission, LLC; City of Cleveland, 
Department of Public Utilities, Division of Cleveland Public Power; City of Hamilton, OH; Dominion Energy 
Services, Inc. on behalf of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy 
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Duke Energy Ohio, Inc., Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc., and Duke Energy Business 
Services LLC; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power Cooperative; Exelon Corporation, on behalf of 
Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, 
Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and 
Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, as agent for its affiliates American Transmission 
Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, Keystone 
Appalachian Transmission Company, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company and Trans-
Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy Transmission Companies”); Old Dominion Electric 
Cooperative; PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Rockland Electric Company; Southern Maryland Electric 
Cooperative, Inc.; UGI Utilities Inc; and Wabash Valley Power Association, Inc.

2 
 
Answer to the March 24, 2025 Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., the March 24, 2025 
Answer of Public Service Electric and Gas Company, and the April 4, 2025 Motion for 
Clarification of Vistra Corp.  Paragraph 87 of the Show Cause Order and the Commission’s 
Ordering Paragraph (D) permit responses by “[i]nterested entities” within “30 days of PJM’s . . . 
filing.”4 
The record in this proceeding demonstrates that the existing PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) remains just and reasonable and that co-
located load is Network Load that uses and relies on the transmission system and should pay for 
transmission service, and other PJM services.  While no changes to the existing PJM Tariff are 
necessary, to the extent FERC believes it would provide helpful clarity, the Indicated TOs 
recommend adopting a proposed definition of co-located load clarifying that it is Network Load, 
so that all parties may proceed with the timely interconnection of co-located arrangements based 
on clear and common understanding of the applicable rates for service.  The definition proposed 
in the Indicated TOs’ initial response accomplishes that goal.  
I. 
Because the Requisite Showing Has Not Been Made Under Federal Power Act 
Section 206, the Commission Should Terminate the Show Cause Proceeding and 
Reaffirm that the Existing PJM Tariff Is Just and Reasonable. 
 
The record in this proceeding demonstrates that the existing PJM Tariff is just and 
reasonable.  Consequently, the legally proper course of action is for the Commission to terminate 
this Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 206 proceeding.  The Commission should act promptly to 
provide interested stakeholders much needed and much desired certainty. 
 
 
4 Show Cause Order, 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 at P 87; see also id. at Ordering Paragraph (D).

3 
 
a. The Existing PJM Tariff Is Just and Reasonable. 
PJM—the administrator of the PJM markets and the PJM Tariff—and virtually all of the 
PJM transmission owners, including investor-owned utilities, municipalities, and cooperatives, are 
in agreement: the “existing Tariff remains just and reasonable.”5  As PJM explains, “[t]he Tariff 
today permits co-located loads to interconnect through existing load interconnection processes.”6  
Those end-use load connection processes, governed by the states and fully consistent with the PJM 
Tariff, are available to all, and those processes work.  Moreover, the transmission service provided 
to co-located load under the PJM Tariff is available to all on a non-discriminatory basis.  Nowhere 
in the record is there an allegation—let alone evidence—that the current PJM Tariff impedes the 
development of or service to any load, co-located or otherwise.  Therefore, there is no basis to alter 
the existing PJM Tariff under section 206 of the FPA.  
In a proceeding under section 206 of the FPA, the Commission can only remedy a “rate 
[or] charge” or “any rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate [or] charge” after it 
is found to be “unjust [or] unreasonable.”7  “The burden of proving an unjust or unreasonable rate 
rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—the Commission [(as in this case)] or the third-
party complainant.”8  Only after a successful showing that the prevailing rate is unjust and 
unreasonable may the Commission order a replacement rate.9  No such showing has been made 
here. 
 
 
5 Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at 4 (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”); see also id. at 32 (“PJM’s Tariff 
remains just and reasonable.”). 
6 Id. at 32. 
7 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a). 
8 Pub. Citizen, Inc. v. FERC, 7 F.4th 1177, 1183 (D.C. Cir. 2021). 
9 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a).

4 
 
Although some entities “may prefer, for their own business reasons, alternative pathways 
to co-location,” business preferences “do not render the [PJM] Tariff unjust and unreasonable.”10  
Nor should PJM develop its rules addressing co-located load specifically to appease or conform to 
a particular entity’s business model.  As the Indicated TOs explained in their Answer, the PJM 
Tariff already has mechanisms to allow co-located load to connect to the grid and ensure that, as 
Network Load, these co-located loads pay for their share of grid services.11  Indeed, PJM’s Answer 
emphasizes the numerous ways in which the existing PJM Tariff ensures just and reasonable rates 
for co-located loads.  As the Indicated TOs explained, and PJM further validated in its answer, 
PJM’s Tariff remains just and reasonable because “co-located load is interconnected with the grid 
and relies on the grid.”12  Just like every other load, those loads connect to and receive service 
from PJM’s transmission system and there is no indication that the PJM Tariff’s construct does not 
work.  Significantly, PJM agrees.13  
While one transmission owner suggests otherwise, citing what it characterizes as 
Commission “skepticism” that existing provisions of the PJM Tariff are appropriate for all types 
 
 
10 PJM Answer at 32. 
11 See Indicated TOs Answer at 14–17 (Mar. 24, 2025).  In appropriate circumstances, the PJM Tariff may alternatively 
permit Point-to-Point Service as an option. 
12 Id. at 13. 
13 See PJM Answer at 4, 32 (stating that the PJM Tariff “remains just and reasonable”); see also id. at 38 (“PJM 
continues to prefer that co-location arrangements be designated ‘Network Load’ in front of the meter.”); id. at 44 
(“Absent an arrangement where both the load and the generator are completely isolated and physically disconnected 
from the grid, (a situation which is very different from the claimed ‘totally isolated’ configuration offered by some in 
these proceedings), PJM is not aware of a configuration that would ‘ensure the co-located load never takes any form 
of transmission service.’  As noted above, grid-connected facilities benefit from their connection and should pay for 
grid services consumed.”).

5 
 
of co-located load configurations,14 “skepticism” is not the standard of proof under section 206 of 
the FPA.  The standard is whether the existing PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable—a showing 
that has not been satisfied. 
b. Behind the Meter Generation Is Not Similarly Situated to Co-Located Load. 
 
Although the vast majority of PJM transmission owners, including traditional transmission 
owners, municipalities and cooperatives are aligned, a single transmission owner also claims that 
“[a]n approach that aligns with cost causation principles is one that treats all co-located customers 
as [Network Integration Transmission Service] customers with netting rules applied” and that “this 
is the current construct for [Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”)] customers under the PJM 
Tariff.”15  Notwithstanding this allegation, the two configurations—BTMG and co-located load—
remain distinct.  Accordingly, reference to behind the meter generation is wholly inapposite to the 
co-located load inquiry here.    
Netting is permitted under the PJM Tariff for BTMG when load takes Network Integration 
Transmission Service (“Network Service”) from a network service customer and the load has its 
own generator.16  Netting occurs when a generator provides power directly to a load and the billing 
determinant used to compute the Network Service costs for that network load is reduced by the 
quantity of power consumption offset by its BTMG.  By way of example, electric cooperatives in 
 
 
14  Response of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to the Order to Show Cause at 10 (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PSEG 
Answer”) (alleging that “[i]t is telling that the Commission acknowledged that while PJM’s preference is that ‘large 
loads be in front of the meter and designated as PJM Network Load,’ the Commission stated that the PJM Tariff does 
not appear to require this service” and that the “Commission expressed skepticism that this is the appropriate type of 
transmission service that should be required of all co-located configurations”). 
15 Id. at 13. 
16 PJM OATT, Section 34.2, Netting of Behind the Meter Generation (“The daily load of a Network Customer does 
not include load served by operating Behind The Meter Generation.  The daily load of a Network Customer shall not 
be reduced by energy injections into the transmission system by the Network Customer.”).

6 
 
particular use BTMG including certain diesel generating facilities to serve load and rely on the 
PJM Tariff provisions that provide for netting of this BTMG for purposes of charges for Network 
Service and other services used to facilitate the public utility service they provide.   
Co-located load is distinct from BTMG.  Were co-located load netted against generation it 
would not be measured as load even though it uses the transmission system.  The PJM Tariff 
provisions on BTMG define it as follows: 
“Behind The Meter Generation” shall refer to a generation unit that 
delivers energy to load without using the Transmission System or 
any distribution facilities (unless the entity that owns or leases the 
distribution facilities has consented to such use of the distribution 
facilities and such consent has been demonstrated to the satisfaction 
of the Office of the Interconnection); provided, however, that 
Behind The Meter Generation does not include (i) at any time, any 
portion of such generating unit’s capacity that is designated as a 
Generation Capacity Resource; or (ii) in an hour, any portion of the 
output of such generating unit that is sold to another entity for 
consumption at another electrical location or into the PJM 
Interchange Energy Market.17 
Because the record in this proceeding is clear that co-located load arrangements do use the 
transmission system, they cannot qualify as BTMG.  Service to co-located load using generators 
connected to the transmission system inherently both use and rely on the transmission system.18   
Treating co-located load similarly to BTMG would result in “the costs assessed” not 
“bear[ing] some resemblance ‘to the burdens imposed or benefits drawn by that party.’”19  To 
 
 
17 PJM OATT, Section 1 (Definitions). 
18 See, e.g., Declaration of David Weaver, PE at PP 10–24, Attach. 1 to Exelon Comments, Docket No. EL25-20 (Dec. 
12, 2024) (“Weaver Decl.”); see also, e.g., id. P 17 (explaining that because nuclear units are unable to provide black 
start services, co-located load must rely on those services from other resources in PJM that are connected to the grid 
in order to come back online); id. P 19 (explaining that the co-located load will take service that is dependent “on a 
strong interconnection with the grid that is supported by reactive power, operating reserves, and black start”). 
19 Pub. Serv. Elec. & Gas Co. v. FERC, 989 F.3d 10, 13 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (quoting Midwest ISO Transmission Owners 
v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368–69 (D.C. Cir. 2004)).

7 
 
afford similar treatment would be to grant an undue preference to such configurations over others 
that also rely upon Network Service.20  Just like all other loads, Network Service should be paid 
when there is co-located load.  To restate: the PJM Tariff and Order No. 888’s pro forma open 
access transmission service tariff contemplate two types—and only two types—of service: (1) 
Network Service for general network service; and (2) Point-to-Point Transmission Service (“Point-
to-Point Service”) for wheeling.  As PJM itself has stated, if you are looking to serve co-located 
load, Network Service is the correct service to take under the Tariff.21 
BTMG and co-located load are not similarly situated.  As PJM explains, BTMG was 
conceived for, and has been implemented for, substantially smaller loads.22  Under the PJM Tariff, 
co-located load is Network Load and should be in front of the meter.  The majority of the 
transmission owners in PJM, inclusive of investor-owned utilities, municipalities, and 
cooperatives, remain aligned that treating co-located load as Network Load is essential for 
reliability, transmission planning, PJM’s procurement of adequate capacity, and appropriate cost-
allocation.23 
The notion that “the data center load could be structured on a front of the meter basis with 
the co-located generator providing primary power and with back-up power coming from the grid; 
or the data center load could be fully isolated behind the meter with system protection facilities in 
 
 
20 See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b) (“No public utility shall, with respect to any transmission or sale subject to the jurisdiction 
of the Commission, (1) make or grant any undue preference or advantage to any person or subject any person to any 
undue prejudice or disadvantage, or (2) maintain any unreasonable difference in rates, charges, service, facilities, or 
in any other respect, either as between localities or as between classes of service.”). 
21 See PJM Answer at 38. 
22 Id. at 13. 
23 Cf. id. at 39 n.64.

8 
 
place to ensure that there is no flow of power from the grid to the load”24 is, at best, inaccurate.  
As explained by the Indicated TOs, there is no such thing as data center load configured to be 
“fully isolated” behind the meter through “system protection facilities,” because co-located load 
that is connected to the electric grid (a) necessarily relies on reliability services, such as ancillary 
services, including black start; (b) retains the potential to draw real or reactive power from the grid 
at any time; and (c) relies on and benefits from its connection to the transmission system at all 
times.25  In other words, there is no such thing as a co-located configuration, connected to and 
synchronized with the electric grid, that is “fully isolated.”  While protection systems may serve 
important roles, they do not isolate the load from the grid, and the grid must be maintained—with 
the attendant costs—to accommodate this reality. 
Indeed, PJM has recognized this, stating that it 
objects to the [Commission’s] use of the phrase “wholly isolated 
from the grid” [in a question] as it is contrary to engineering and 
economic principles.  The notion that any of the proposed co-
location arrangements can be “wholly isolated” is misleading.  The 
load and generator are connected to and synchronized with the 
multi-state bulk power system.  It is not operating as a micro grid 
(nor can it if the generating facility is a nuclear unit).  Nor is the 
generator delivering power through an intermediary to a load with a 
breaker open.  Further, by way of example, there are obligations to 
ensure power to nuclear plants to ensure safe shutdown (among 
other things).  The load and generator are benefiting from ancillary 
services (including but not limited to black start).  Any system 
protection facilities are designed to only handle less complex N-1 
conditions, and can misoperate (and indeed have misoperated).26 
 
 
24 PSEG Answer at 11. 
25 See Indicated TOs Answer, Attach. (A) at 4–5. 
26 PJM Answer at 42–43.

9 
 
 
PJM also explained that, 
 
[a]bsent an arrangement where both the load and the generator are 
completely isolated and physically disconnected from the grid, (a 
situation which is very different from the claimed “totally isolated” 
configuration offered by some in these proceedings), PJM is not 
aware of a configuration that would “ensure the co-located load 
never takes any form of transmission service.”  As noted above, 
grid-connected facilities benefit from their connection and should 
pay for grid services consumed.27  
 
In other words, transmission services are being provided to and relied upon by the co-located load 
whether or not it is behind the meter.  The PJM Tariff allows for service to co-located load as 
Network Service.  Such treatment is needed in order to ensure reliability, effective transmission 
planning, procurement of adequate capacity, and proper cost allocation. 
II. 
No Replacement Rate Is Necessary or Appropriate Under FPA Section 206. 
a. PJM’s Potential Options Are Unnecessary to Resolve the Show Cause 
Proceeding. 
 
The Indicated TOs appreciate PJM laying out several “potential options for additional large 
load co-location.”28  However, it is important to emphasize that the mere presentation of potential 
options does not establish that the existing PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable and therefore 
cannot be the basis upon which to impose a replacement rate.  In this case, moreover, the options 
are not of all one kind—some are fully available options now; others are not practical.  In fact, 
four of the eight—options 1, 2, 3, and 8 (described below)—are currently available without any 
 
 
27 Id. at 44. 
28 Id. at 5.

10 
 
changes to the existing PJM Tariff.29  In contrast, the record in this proceeding demonstrates that 
the potential options that would require changes to the PJM Tariff are unnecessary and have not 
been shown to be just and reasonable.  Therefore, no changes to the PJM Tariff may be directed 
under FPA section 206 in this docket.  Indeed, PJM itself asserts that its tariff “remains just and 
reasonable.”30 
The potential options PJM presents are as follows: 
1. Load with a separate Point of Interconnection that is Network Load and the load uses 
and pays for Network Service, Energy, Ancillary Services, and Capacity.  
2. Co-located load that is at the same Point of Interconnection but separately metered that 
is Network Load and the load uses and pays for Network Service, Energy, Ancillary 
Services, and Capacity.  Additionally, the large load is studied and could be connected 
to the grid pursuant to the existing Transmission Owner/electric distribution company 
(“EDC”) load interconnection process. 
3. Existing BTMG where the load is the customer, the BTMG rules apply, and the load 
uses and pays for Network Service, Energy, Ancillary Services, and Capacity based on 
the net withdrawal quantity and dependent on if that withdrawal is during the Peak. 
4. Co-located load with connection to the grid with protections to avoid delivery of system 
energy to serve the load, but relies on and takes grid services such as ancillary services 
and should pay its fair share of those charges, and carries a risk that should system 
protections fail, significant energy would be drawn from the system.  
 
 
29 PJM asserts that three of the options “already exist under PJM’s Tariff.”  Id.  Of course, only those that meet the 
tariff criteria would be eligible for the options.  For example, to participate in a demand response program, the load 
would need to satisfy the various tariff criteria for demand response. 
30 Id. at 4, 32.

11 
 
5. Co-located load with connection to the grid with protections to avoid delivery of system 
energy to load (same as option 4) but allowed to use back-up service from PJM with 
permission.  Like option 4, it relies on and takes grid services such as ancillary services 
and should pay its fair share of those charges, and carries a risk that should system 
protections fail, significant energy would be drawn from the system. 
6. Co-located load that elects to be Network Load and bring its own generation where 
large load additions interconnecting as Network Load could also bring to PJM 
additional generation that could serve as Capacity Resources. 
7. Potential new non-capacity backed service as a Transitional Service, with a co-location 
configuration where load is curtailable. 
8. Co-located load participating in Demand Response, where load is Network Load and 
participates as a Demand Response resource. 
PJM’s options reinforce the straightforward conclusion that the existing PJM Tariff is just 
and reasonable.  Options 1, 2, 3, and 8 all lay out fact patterns for load that meets the needs 
identified in this docket for co-located load.  Options 1 and 2 make clear that the addition of load 
at or near generation, whether or not it shares the same points of interconnection as a generator, 
can be accomplished quickly and easily.  The load simply needs to agree to pay for the services 
that all load receives and take service as Network Load.  No tariff amendments are needed to add 
load to the system.  Some commenters have claimed that netting load and generation that share an 
interconnection is an important option for co-located load.31  Indeed, Option 3 demonstrates that a 
path to netting exists under the PJM Tariff, if in fact the particular arrangement has been configured 
 
 
31 See PSEG Answer at 13.

12 
 
so that it does qualify as BTMG, as defined under the PJM Tariff.  Other entities have argued that 
co-located load can provide benefits to the system by relying on back-up generation or otherwise 
leaving the system under certain circumstances.  As Option 8 shows, demand response is a well-
established regime for compensating load that agrees not to call on the system when required.  No 
new tariff provisions are needed to accomplish that goal. 
PJM’s options make clear the high burden presented by FPA section 206 is not met here.  
For example, if co-located load wishes to be compensated for being interruptible, at the 
transmission level,32 advocates of that position need to show why that outcome is the correct rate 
design and why the current demand response rules fail to adequately compensate load 
appropriately.  Such a showing has not been made for any of the currently available Tariff options.  
Accordingly, PJM’s potential options that would require changes to the PJM Tariff do not present 
a viable replacement rate, and PJM has not argued otherwise.  Indeed, PJM notes that it “does not 
mean to suggest that all identified ‘options’ . . . are equivalent, desirable, or even necessarily 
workable.”33    
b. Changes to the PJM Tariff May Undercut Reliability. 
 
The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) has warned of impending 
reliability challenges that will attend the increased demand growth in PJM.34  This is important 
because the reasonableness of a rate, including any replacement rate set under FPA section 206, 
“is assessed in light of the FPA’s goals of promoting reliable service at reasonable rates and 
 
 
32 States, which regulate the general terms and conditions governing service to co-located end-use load, can and do 
offer optional or mandatory interruptible service rates. 
33 PJM Answer at 5. 
34 See Indicated TOs Answer at 3–4 (discussing NERC’s 2024 Long-Term Reliability Assessment).

13 
 
developing plentiful energy supplies.”35  To treat co-located load as anything other than Network 
Load would increase the risk of reliability failures and resource inadequacy in PJM.  As PJM 
explained in its filing, “[i]f the co-located load is PJM Network Load, PJM and the Transmission 
Owners have means through existing Tariff provisions and agreements to obtain the information 
to have both sufficient visibility and sufficient control of this load and ensure the load could be 
served reliably without compromising overall system reliability.”36  When co-located load is 
hidden and not appropriately accounted for, however, there is not only a cost-allocation problem, 
but the study process is undermined and, consequently, PJM may be unable to adequately procure 
enough capacity to serve the load because the full load will not be accounted for in the Reliability 
Pricing Model.  Nor would the full load be reliably and safely factored into both PJM’s 
transmission planning and operations processes and protocols. 
The Commission must prioritize the safety and reliability of the electric grid.   
c. The Potential Options that Require Changes to the PJM Tariff Would Slow 
Data Center Development, the Opposite of What the Commission Should 
Encourage. 
 
As PJM and the Indicated TOs have asserted, the PJM Tariff remains just and reasonable, 
and no party has shown that the existing PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable.  As such, the 
Commission has no basis under FPA section 206 to implement any proposed changes to the PJM 
Tariff.  Moreover, recognizing that several of PJM’s proposed options are wholly consistent with 
the existing PJM Tariff further supports the Commission in providing additional guidance and 
 
 
35 Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1035 (D.C. Cir. 2022).   
36 PJM Answer at 61.

14 
 
certainty through an order either stating affirmatively that is the case or simply terminating this 
proceeding.37     
The need to provide power to large load customers is clear and the best way to promote co-
located large load customers is to provide all stakeholders—inclusive of customers, EDCs/load 
serving entities, transmission owners, and investors—with certainty, which the Commission can 
quickly accomplish by clarifying that co-located loads should seek service under the well-
established, just and reasonable terms of the existing PJM Tariff.  It is also worth noting that any 
attempt to change the PJM Tariff would likely stymie data-center development, as such 
hypothetical new terms would require development through the PJM stakeholder process followed 
by Commission consideration and acceptance.  But no new terms are required.  The PJM Tariff 
already allows co-located load to interconnect to the grid and rely on the grid as Network Load.  
State-jurisdictional special contracts or rates can continue to provide other financial benefits to the 
co-located load.  But pursuing drastic changes to the PJM Tariff will only increase uncertainty—
not just about the development of infrastructure for large load customers but about the future of 
the very grid that desperately needs development, a task that is only made more difficult when 
certainty and regulatory clarity are undermined.  Not even PJM knows how its options would be 
affected by other provisions of the PJM Tariff.  As noted above, by its own admission, PJM’s 
proposed new options have not been vetted to determine if they are “desirable, or even necessarily 
workable.”38   
 
 
37 As explained above, to the extent to which the Commission thinks it would be helpful to have further clarity in the 
PJM Tariff, the Indicated TOs suggest considering whether the addition of their proposed co-located load definition 
would improve the PJM Tariff.  
38 Id. at 5.

15 
 
III. 
Vistra’s Motion for Clarification Should Be Denied. 
On April 4, 2025, Vistra filed a Motion for Clarification and Request for Expedited 
Treatment.  Vistra seeks the Commission’s interpretation of its order issued in November 2024 in 
Docket No. ER24-2172 (“Susquehanna ISA Proceeding”).39  According to Vistra, there is 
confusion on the scope and holding of the Susquehanna ISA Order.  The Commission should reject 
Vistra’s motion.  
In the Susquehanna ISA Proceeding, the Commission rejected the amended 
interconnection agreement between Susquehanna Nuclear LLC, PJM, and PPL Electric Utilities 
Corporation because the Commission found that “PJM has not demonstrated that the proposed   
non-conforming provisions in the Amended ISA are necessary deviations from the pro forma ISA 
due to specific reliability concerns, novel legal issues, or other unique factors.”40 
On April 10, 2025, the Commission issued in Docket No. ER24-2172, an Order Addressing 
Arguments on Rehearing and Granting Clarification, In Part.41  Therein, the Commission 
addressed Vistra’s request for clarification in the Susquehanna ISA Proceeding.  In Susquehanna 
ISA Rehearing Order, the Commission clarified that it “uses the necessary standard . . . to 
determine whether the filing of a non-conforming agreement is justified” and that the Susquehanna 
ISA Order “does not prevent entities from filing non-conforming interconnection agreements to 
address matters related to a generator serving co-located load, or prejudge any such future filing.”42  
 
 
39 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078 (2024) (“Susquehanna ISA Order”). 
40 Id. P 85. 
41 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,025 (2025) (“Susquehanna ISA Rehearing Order”). 
42 Id. P 30.

16 
 
Therefore, Vistra’s request for clarification has been addressed and the April 4th motion submitted 
in this proceeding is moot. 
No further clarification is needed in this proceeding.  Any attempt by Vistra to seek further 
clarification in this proceeding would amount to Vistra asking the Commission to tell PJM to alter 
its view on what is permissible under the PJM Tariff.  That is not an appropriate basis for the 
Commission to grant its motion for clarification in the instant proceeding. 
IV. 
Conclusion 
For the reasons stated above, the Indicated TOs respectfully request that the Commission 
find that the existing PJM Tariff is just and reasonable, that co-located load can be served with the 
existing forms of transmission service in the PJM Tariff, and that the Commission accordingly 
terminate this FPA section 206 proceeding and the above-captioned dockets. 
 
Respectfully submitted,
